name: Priya Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential; I’d like both what you would say openly and what you think privately. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Priya, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company that builds software for connecting homes to broadband networks. I have a bachelor’s degree and handle ordinary provisioning faults, while a specialist takes the hardest network cases. I check failed orders, trace which address or line was entered wrongly, and test the fix before a crew is sent. I have never used an AI tool; I want to see the address and the line record myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does this work support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Martin, is a carpenter, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My developer pay is high for this job; we have about eleven months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar jobs nearby. We lived in a smaller place for years to build that reserve, so I will not spend it casually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau leaves us checking each network order before a crew goes to the wrong house. A routine sorter could help, but it should not invent an address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be comfortable about my job and the mortgage. Eleven months saved and Martin’s carpentry income give us room for ordinary setbacks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking failed orders against the address register and have a specialist review unusual line faults. I’d continue putting 550 into savings each month while both incomes hold. In the first year I’d ask crews to keep reporting wrong-address calls so we can fix the root cause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our money, though I still dislike sending a crew on a wasted trip. I do not expect this picture to reduce my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which wrong address stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A crew once drove across town because a flat number had been dropped. I found the missing digit in the old order and stopped the next visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the house plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Martin we can keep saving for the children’s future lessons, but we do not need a bigger house now. A buffer is more useful than an extra room.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking network orders.
I would reject **invented addresses** before sending a crew.
think: I expect my **job and mortgage** to remain secure.
Our **eleven-month reserve** and carpentry pay give us room for setbacks.
do: **Keep** checking failed network orders against the address register.
**Collect** crew reports of wrong-address calls for root-cause fixes.
feel: **Calm** about income, with concern for wasted crew visits.
S0.quote: A crew once drove across town because a flat number had been dropped.
fieldNote: Her **address checks** prevented a repeat wasted crew visit after a missing flat number.
High pay, **eleven months saved** and many nearby openings support current job security.

steps.text: Keep checking network orders against addresses and crew reports
Save 550 monthly while both incomes hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let software check orders, draft fixes and answer customers much faster. I would ask our crews to test the new checker before management changes staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our company may keep fewer developers for ordinary provisioning faults. My own job could shrink even with a good record, though Martin’s hands-on carpentry should change more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our network specialist to run the approved AI checker on sixteen old wrong-address orders while I compare crew notes. If it catches all sixteen, I’d learn its review screen during paid time. In the first year, if the firm cuts developer posts, I’d ask our trade association to gather affected workers for a meeting about notice and training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, despite our savings. Eleven months of savings would soften a cut, not replace a dependable wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the crew supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the flat-number case to the crew supervisor and ask who signs the address before dispatch. The crew loses a day if the software guesses wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children that Martin’s work may keep going, but I would not promise my company will keep every developer. We could hold off on the next big house project.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed orders, fixes and customer replies.
I would ask **crews to test** the checker before staffing changes.
think: I fear **fewer developers** will handle routine faults.
I think Martin’s **carpentry work** changes more slowly than my code.
do: **Test** the approved checker against sixteen old wrong-address orders.
**Learn** its review screen during paid time only if all sixteen pass.
**Convene** affected workers through the trade association if developer posts are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours despite a long savings buffer.
S1.quote: Eleven months of savings would soften a cut, not replace a dependable wage.
fieldNote: She accepts an **approved tool** only after sixteen crew-checked orders pass and paid learning time is available.
Her **association meeting** depends on actual developer cuts; carpentry income gives some household continuity.

steps.text: Learn approved network checker during paid time if sixteen old cases pass
Convene affected workers through trade association if developer posts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches network-code thinking work in 2028. Hands-on robots come around 2031, so Martin’s carpentry may get more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect much of our provisioning code team could go, including me. Eleven months saved is helpful, but those developer vacancies nearby may shrink together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for written severance and keep the planned home-extension money in cash. I’d list real local technical vacancies and ask Martin what projects he could safely take without overworking. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to actual openings and draw from savings for the mortgage while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large loss of my pay before we know what carpentry will look like three years later. I have time to search, but eleven months saved cannot guarantee another developer job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the extension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children we are not starting the extension while my job is uncertain. The current bedrooms work, even if they complain about sharing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family help be available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my sister whether she could watch the children for interviews if she has time. I would not ask her to replace my salary or Martin’s carpentry work.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach network code before carpentry robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Martin’s **hands-on work** may change later.
think: I expect my **code team** could shrink sharply.
I cannot assume **nearby developer vacancies** survive full thinking AI.
do: **Delay** the home extension and hold its cash for the mortgage.
**Request** written severance and list real local technical openings now.
**Apply** for actual vacancies if dismissed after 2028, asking my sister for childcare if available.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected pay loss despite eleven months of savings.
S2.quote: I have time to search, but eleven months saved cannot guarantee another developer job.
fieldNote: She correctly faces the **2028 code shock** before hands-on robots around 2031.
Her **sister’s childcare** is conditional; she will not treat family money or nearby vacancies as guaranteed.

steps.text: Delay home extension and hold the money for mortgage bills
Apply to actual local vacancies if dismissed after 2028
Ask sister for interview childcare only if she has time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to learn how crews really handle network faults. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031; hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer code jobs, but I can learn more about field checks while earning. I will not call field checks a safe new trade, because robots follow three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our crew supervisor for one approved morning monthly on wrong-address calls and learn how they verify a line on site. I’d use the free network safety manual if the company refuses the time. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d apply only for real field-support vacancies paying enough for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the coding role, with more time to test a skill than in 2028. I would keep the extension fund as cash until we see real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove a field skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the crew supervisor to mark one site-check report I wrote. If I confuse the line number, I need more practice before claiming field skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for certification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for a certificate with no actual opening attached. The free manual and one approved morning are enough to find out whether I can do the job.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to learn real crew checks.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect **fewer coding roles** despite the warning.
I cannot assume **field support** stays safe once robots arrive.
do: **Learn** site line checks monthly with supervisor feedback if crew time is approved.
**Study** the free safety manual if company time is refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying field support jobs if code ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about code income, with time to test another skill.
S3.quote: I will not call field checks a safe new trade, because robots follow three years later.
fieldNote: She uses the **five-year window** to test field work without claiming it survives 2034 robots.
Her **site morning** requires approval; any job move requires a vacancy and mortgage-covering pay.

steps.text: Learn monthly site checks with supervisor feedback if approved; otherwise study free safety manual
Apply for actual field-support roles covering mortgage if code ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to improve the network records crews use. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay to hold for now, and our reserve means we can plan without rushing. I still want managers to keep experienced people who can explain old network lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking provisioning orders against crew notes and save 550 monthly while both wages hold. I’d take one work-funded network safety class if the company offers it. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d search actual vacancies and compare pay before moving the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long view, but I feel secure in the near term. Ten years gives us time to teach the children to value a skill they can demonstrate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about skills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Martin to show our children how he measures a door frame before cutting wood. Careful work is more than clicking a button. They should see that in his carpentry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you restart the house project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would not start a larger house project without a written budget and stable wages. If my code job ends, a real job offer must cover housing before we move.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to improve crew records.
I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect my **pay** to hold for now.
I want **experienced staff** kept to explain old network lines.
do: **Keep** checking network orders and save 550 monthly while both wages hold.
**Take** a work-funded network safety class only if offered.
**Search** actual vacancies after 2036 if coding ends, comparing pay before moving.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-term work, with secure near-term income.
S4.quote: Careful work is more than clicking a button.
fieldNote: Her **long runway** supports teaching practical skills and a funded class without risking savings.
The **house project** needs stable wages and a budget; a move needs a real affordable offer.

steps.text: Keep checking network orders against crew notes
Save 550 monthly while both wages hold
Take a work-funded network safety class if offered
Search real vacancies after 2036 coding loss; compare offered pay and housing before moving children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because code work could vanish before we know what happens to Martin’s carpentry. Written severance, paid time to learn crew checks and real vacancies would help. My sister might watch the children for interviews, but she cannot provide a replacement wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who arrives at the wrong house when a line record is bad. The crew has to face the person at the door, not the dashboard.

headlineQuote: The crew has to face the person at the door, not the dashboard.
portrait: Priya is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, high pay and eleven months of expenses saved.
She has **never used AI** and traces broadband order faults through address records before sending crews.
Her partner’s **carpentry** is hands-on, with robots arriving roughly three years after thinking AI reaches her code.
She seeks **approved crew learning**, actual jobs and conditional sibling childcare while holding house-extension cash.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her code income before carpentry robots affect her partner’s trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid learning and real vacancies would help.
